title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? The language \(\mathrm{GNI}\) consists of valid encodings of two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs. This asks whether \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
why: This asks whether random computation alone can efficiently decide a canonical structural equivalence problem. Nonisomorphism has efficient interactive verification, but the help of an unbounded prover is an additional resource. Settling the BPP question would locate ordinary graph comparison more precisely between efficient deterministic algorithms, randomized algorithms and stronger forms of verification.
status_note: Explicitly open as a BPP question in Goldreich’s April 2017 manuscript. The corrected general upper bound and the full introduction of Neuen’s 2026 survey were checked, alongside targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026. No verified general BPP algorithm or separation was found. The 2026 deterministic-status statement is not being used as a theorem about BPP, and the bounded search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

importance.reason: A central randomized-computation variant of graph isomorphism, distinguished from both the deterministic polynomial-time frontier and interactive proof membership.

sentences: Graph nonisomorphism asks whether two graphs have no adjacency-preserving vertex bijection.
The target is one randomized polynomial-time algorithm with error at most one third on every encoded input.
Because BPP is closed under complement, the same question can be phrased for ordinary graph isomorphism.
Interactive proofs, quasipolynomial algorithms and algorithms for restricted graph classes do not provide the required decider.
A resolution would clarify whether random computation alone suffices for this central structural comparison problem.

definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. At a randomized transition the machine may obtain one independent unbiased random bit, with this transition counted in its runtime. Success probability is over these internal bits for each fixed input, not over a distribution of graphs. BPP consists of binary languages for which such a machine has error at most \(1/3\) on every input and a polynomial worst-case clock over inputs and random outcomes. For \(\mathrm{GNI}\), acceptance is required with probability at least \(2/3\) when the encoding is valid and \(G\not\cong H\); it is at most \(1/3\) for isomorphic pairs and malformed strings. Distinct vertex counts form yes-instances for GNI. The output is only one membership bit, without a nonisomorphism certificate, quantum computation or interaction with another party. One machine and one polynomial must work at all graph sizes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\) or \(\mathrm{GNI}\notin\mathrm{BPP}\) in the model above. The positive case must supply one uniform polynomial-time bounded-error decider, or establish its existence, with the required probability bound on every input. The negative case must exclude every such randomized machine. Correctness only on typical graphs, an interactive verification protocol, a method with only expected polynomial time and no suitable clock conversion, or a restricted-model lower bound does not by itself settle this target.

context_blocks.text: Graph nonisomorphism asserts that no bijection of the vertex sets preserves adjacency. An isomorphism is an easily checked witness for the opposite answer; a failed attempt to find one does not certify nonisomorphism. The target requires a bounded probability of error on every graph pair, including highly symmetric instances.

Goldreich’s footnote uses graph nonisomorphism to contrast an interactive proof with a problem not known to have a BPP algorithm. The verifier in such a proof receives messages from a computationally unbounded party. The question here removes that assistance and asks about the verifier’s own randomized computation.

BPP is closed under complement: reversing the answer preserves its error bound and runtime. After checking that the encoding is valid, an algorithm for nonisomorphism can therefore be turned into one for isomorphism, and conversely. Validity checking is needed because both graph languages reject malformed strings. Thus this is exactly the randomized polynomial-time question for ordinary graph isomorphism, with its answer polarity reversed.

The deterministic and randomized targets are related but distinct. A deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider supplies a positive answer here. A negative answer here would exclude a deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider and, since isomorphism has efficiently checkable permutation witnesses, would imply P differs from NP. A positive answer here does not automatically derandomize the computation.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.
